newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan top court delivers setback to war shrine.
newsitem.headline: Japan top court delivers setback to war shrine.

text.p: Japan's Supreme Court, in a landmark ruling on the separation of state and religion, said on Wednesday the use of taxpayers' money for offerings at a controversial war shrine was unconstitutional.

The 15-member Grand Bench ruled 13-to-two that cash offerings by a local government to Tokyo's Yasukuni Shrine, where 2.6 million war dead from World War Two and previous conflicts are enshrined, violated constitutional provisions separating state and religion.
It ordered local authorities in Ehime Prefecture, 720 km (450 miles) southwest of Tokyo, to pay back to the prefecture 166,000 yen ($1,360) in offerings they made at Shinto shrines from 1981 to 1986.

Shinto, Japan's ancient animistic religion, was the state religion until 1945, with the emperor as its spiritual head. Visitors to a Shinto shrine by tradition give cash gifts as forms of tribute to the enshrined gods.
The offerings were challenged in 1982, when 24 Ehime residents complained they violated the constitution and filed a suit demanding the cash be repaid to public coffers.
"It was a landmark ruling for the Supreme Court which had traditionally called similar cases constitutional," said Hiroshi Itakura, professor of law at Nihon University.
Article 20 of Japan's U.S.-imposed constitution says no religious organisation may receive any privileges from the state and the state should refrain from religious activity.
"I'm happy that the ruling reconfirmed the fundamental principle of Japan's pacifist constitution," Kenji Yasunishi, the leader of the plaintiff group, told reporters.
Yasukuni Shrine declined to comment on the ruling.

Wednesday's decision was based on a 1977 Supreme Court ruling which said it was impossible to clearly separate state and religion and that actions by the state should be judged on whether the purpose behind the action was of a religious nature or one widely accepted by social custom.
"It is unlikely that the ordinary person will evaluate the offerings in the current case as a social practice," the Supreme Court said in Wednesday's ruling.

Yasukuni Shrine, where wartime prime minister Hideki Tojo and other military leaders hanged by allied forces as war criminals are among those symbolically enshrined as Shinto deities, has often been the focus of controversy.

Last July, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, breaking a decade-long taboo on visits by prime ministers to the shrine, made a "private" visit on his birthday and sparked sharp criticism from China, South Korea and other countries.
"I think today's decision gave a good impression to Asia and other countries who still bear a grudge against Japan's wartime aggression," said Setsu Kobayashi, professor of law at Keio University.
Legal analysts said Wednesday's ruling was likely to make politicians more cautious in visiting the shrine in the future, but not enough to prevent them from going.
"The ruling won't totally discourage the politicians since the demand (to visit Yasukuni) from the families of the deceased is still strong," Itakura said.
Government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said the ruling would not affect visits by ministers to the shrine on August 15, the date of Japan's World War Two surrender.
"The ruling is not about official visits by ministers to the shrine and we don't use public spending for the offerings in official visits," Kajiyama told a news conference.
